title: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling
summary: Bigger machine or more machines? Learn why availability often tips the balance early, where shared state must live and which bottleneck comes next.
body:
Every scaling conversation starts with the same fork: make one machine bigger, or add more machines. The answer shapes everything downstream — your data model, your failure modes, and what you are allowed to promise a user.

## Vertical scaling (scale up)

Buy a bigger box. More cores, more RAM, faster disks. Nothing about the application has to change: the same process, the same in-memory state, the same single database connection pool.

This is genuinely the right answer more often than interview folklore suggests. A single modern server can handle tens of thousands of simple requests per second and hold hundreds of gigabytes to a few terabytes of RAM. Vertical scaling buys you that without introducing a network hop between components that used to be a function call.

It stops working for two reasons, and only one of them is about capacity:

- **There is a ceiling.** The largest instance your cloud sells is a hard wall, and price grows faster than capability as you approach it.
- **There is no redundancy.** One machine is one failure domain. Scaling up does not improve availability at all — it concentrates it.

That second point is what usually forces the decision. Teams move horizontally long before they run out of vertical headroom, because they need to survive losing a machine.

## Horizontal scaling (scale out)

Run many identical instances behind a load balancer. Capacity becomes roughly linear in machine count, and losing one instance degrades throughput instead of causing an outage.

The cost is that your application must become **stateless**. Any request has to be serviceable by any instance, which means per-user state cannot live in process memory:

| State that used to be local | Where it goes |
| --- | --- |
| Session data | Shared cache (Redis) or a signed token |
| Uploaded files | Object storage (S3) |
| In-memory cache | Distributed cache, or accept per-instance duplication |
| Background timers | A scheduler or queue with leader election |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U["Clients"] --> LB["Load balancer"]
    LB --> A1["App 1"]
    LB --> A2["App 2"]
    LB --> A3["App 3"]
    A1 --> R[("Redis: sessions")]
    A2 --> R
    A3 --> R
    A1 --> DB[("Primary database")]
    A2 --> DB
    A3 --> DB
    A1 --> OS[("Object storage")]
```

Any app instance can serve any request because the state it needs lives in shared stores: sessions in Redis, durable records in the database, files in object storage (every instance uses it; one arrow is drawn for clarity). Losing App 2 costs a third of capacity, not users' sessions. Every arrow now converges on the database, which is the point of the next paragraph.

Once state is externalised, the database becomes the bottleneck you have not solved yet. Ten web servers all talk to one primary. Scaling the stateless tier is the easy half; scaling the stateful tier is the topic that fills the rest of this module.

## What scales next

Once the stateless tier scales out, pressure moves to state. Match the technique to the pressure: repeated reads go to a cache or read replicas; write volume or data size calls for partitioning; slow side effects move behind a queue; static and media bytes go to object storage and a CDN. Autoscaling the app tier on CPU or request rate helps with daily traffic curves, but it reacts in minutes and can multiply database connections, so pool connections and cap instance counts.

Common mistakes: scaling out an app that still keeps sessions in memory (users are logged out on every deploy), adding app servers to fix a database-bound endpoint, and claiming "infinite scale" without naming the next bottleneck.

## How to answer this in an interview

Do not open with "we will scale horizontally." Open with the number. Estimate requests per second and working-set size, then state the threshold:

> At 500 RPS and a 40 GB working set, one instance is comfortable. I would still run three behind a load balancer for availability rather than capacity, because a single node means a single outage.

That answer shows you can size a system *and* that you know availability, not throughput, is usually what forces the architecture.

## Further reading

- [The Twelve-Factor App: Processes](https://12factor.net/processes) explains why stateless, share-nothing processes scale horizontally.
keyTakeaways: Vertical scaling needs no application change but has a hard ceiling and zero redundancy.
Availability, not throughput, is usually what forces horizontal scaling.
Scaling out requires statelessness: sessions, files and timers must move out of process memory.
Scaling the stateless tier just relocates the bottleneck to the database.
